modern_lens_framing: The Qurʾan is taken here as fixed, revealed truth; science is our provisional, evolving account of the observable world. What follows notes where the two meet — a contemplation, not a proof. Where the science later shifts, that reflects the limits of our knowledge, not the text.

84:22.title: Persistent Denial, Painful Tidings
84:22.in_short: The disbelievers' real problem is stubborn denial, not missing evidence. Allah knows exactly what they hide in their hearts, and the Prophet ﷺ is told to give them news, bitterly ironic news, of a painful punishment.

claims.text: The word 'bal' (nay/rather) marks a rhetorical turn: the passage moves from wondering why they do not believe to simply stating the fact that they persist in denial, since nothing stops them from believing after every proof has stood confirmed.

sources.original_excerpt: إضرب انتقالى، من التعجيب من عدم إيمانهم... إلى الإِخبار عنهم بأنهم مستمرون على كفرهم

claims.text: What they deny is identified as Muhammad ﷺ and what he brought, the Qur'an, and the resurrection.

sources.original_excerpt: بل الذين كفروا يكذبون بآيات الله وتنـزيله
بالقرآن والبعث
بل الذين كفروا يكذبون محمدا - صلى الله عليه وسلم - وما جاء به

claims.text: On the occasion of revelation, one report (from Muqatil) says the verse came about four men of Banu ʿAmr ibn ʿUmayr, two of whom later became Muslim. Another view holds it addresses disbelievers in general.

sources.original_excerpt: نزلت في بني عمرو بن عمير وكانوا أربعة، فأسلم اثنان منهم. وقيل: هي في جميع الكفار

report.graded_by: al-Qurṭubī (relaying Muqātil, without further isnād evaluation)

claims.text: The denial described here is not a passing lapse but their settled character: rejection, obstinacy, and opposition to the truth. Persisting in disbelief despite clear indications makes a person deserving of the punishment that follows.

sources.original_excerpt: meaning, from their mannerism is rejection, obstinacy, and opposition to the truth.
يعاندون الحق بعدما تبين
جھٹلانا ان کا مزاج ثانی بن گیا ہے

claims.text: Al-Saʿdī says one who denies the truth out of sheer obstinacy, after it has already become clear, cannot be reasoned with. Their disbelief and refusal to submit to the Qur'an should not, therefore, come as a surprise.

sources.original_excerpt: فإن المكذب بالحق عنادًا، لا حيلة فيه.

claims.text: Israr Ahmad distinguishes kufr from takdhib as two separate offences, not synonyms. Kufr literally means 'to conceal': a person buries the innate testimonies Allah placed within human nature about Himself. Takdhib means denying the revealed signs sent to awaken that same inner testimony. On this reading takdhib is the graver crime, since it comes after clear proof and admits no excuse. He points to the charter given to Adam (عليه السلام) in the Qur'an, where 'kafaru' and 'kadhdhabu' are named as distinct wrongs.

sources.original_excerpt: کفر کے لغوی معنی چھپانے کے ہیں... تکذیب سے مراد اللہ تعالیٰ کی ان آیات کو جھٹلانا ہے

claims.text: The word 'yuʿuna' is glossed by Mujahid as 'they conceal' (yaktumun), referring to what they hide in their chests.

sources.original_excerpt: قوله: (يوعون) قال: يكتمون
قال مجاهد: يكتمون
Mujahid and Qatadah both said, 'What they conceal in their chests.'

claims.text: Qatada located this concealment 'in their breasts' - what they hide in their hearts of denial even though they know the truth; a similar sense is reported from Ibn Abbas through al-Dahhak.

sources.original_excerpt: عن قتادة، في قوله: (يوعون) قال في صدورهم
أي بما يضمرونه في أنفسهم من التكذيب. كذا روى الضحاك عن ابن عباس

claims.text: Ibn Zayd reads the verse through its root meaning: just as a person stores his goods and wealth in a container, so hearts are a vessel that gathers all deeds, good and evil, and Allah knows everything they hold.

sources.original_excerpt: المرء يوعي متاعه وماله... فالقلوب وعاء هذه الأعمال كلها، الخير والشر

claims.text: Al-Qurtubi traces 'yuʿuna' to al-wiʿaʾ, the vessel that gathers what is put in it, and cites a line of poetry contrasting how good deeds endure while evil is 'the worst thing you can store as provision'; he adds that waʿa also means 'to memorise/retain', as in 'I retained the report' (waʿaytu al-hadith).

sources.original_excerpt: الخير أبقى وإن طال الزمان به والشر أخبث ما أوعيت من زاد

claims.text: Al-Saʿdī reads the verse as what they do and intend in secret: Allah knows their secret and their open behaviour alike, and will recompense them accordingly.

sources.original_excerpt: أي: بما يعملونه وينوونه سرًا، فالله يعلم سرهم وجهرهم، وسيجازيهم بأعمالهم

claims.text: Tantawi notes the clause is a parenthetical insertion between what comes before and after it, meant as a threat and a warning.

sources.original_excerpt: كلام معترض بين سابقه ولا حقه، والمقصود به التهديد والوعيد

claims.text: Israr Ahmad says the verse is often taken to mean people hoarding wealth, but it actually refers to the impurity filling their hearts and chests: disbelief, enmity, malice, envy, and arrogance, which is why they deny the signs even after recognising them.

sources.original_excerpt: عام طور پر اس آیت کے بارے میں یہی سمجھا گیا ہے کہ اس میں انسان کے مال و دولت جمع کرنے کی طرف اشارہ ہے، لیکن دراصل اس سے دلوں اور سینوں کی گندگی مراد ہے

claims.text: 'Bashshirhum' (give them tidings) is used here as bitter irony: the word normally announces good news, but here it announces painful torment.

sources.original_excerpt: أي أجعل ذلك بمنزلة البشارة
والمراد به هنا التهكم بهم

claims.text: Al-Saʿdī explains that 'bishara' (glad tidings) is so named because it visibly affects the 'bashara' (the skin/outer appearance) with either joy or grief, so the word can properly carry news of pain as well as news of pleasure. He notes this describes the condition of most people: denying the Qur'an and lacking faith in it.

sources.original_excerpt: وسميت البشارة بشارة، لأنها تؤثر في البشرة سرورًا أو غمًا

claims.text: Sayyid Qutb calls this the worst kind of 'good news': news that holds no joy, that nobody wants, and that nobody waits for, unlike the reward prepared for believers who are exempted from this fate through righteous deeds.

sources.original_excerpt: کیا ہی بری خوشخبری ہے جس میں کوئی مسرت نہیں

claims.text: The command is addressed to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: he is told to inform the deniers of the painful punishment Allah has prepared for them.

sources.original_excerpt: فبشر يا محمد هؤلاء المكذّبين بآيات الله بعذاب أليم لهم عند الله موجع
فبشرهم -أيها الرسول- بأن الله عز وجل قد أعدَّ لهم عذابًا موجعًا

84:22.essay_html:
The passage turns on a single word, 'nay' (bal). It signals a shift: rather than ask why the disbelievers do not believe, the verse simply states the fact of their persistence in denial. There is nothing left to stop them believing, once every proof has stood confirmed.9 What they deny is spelled out as Muhammad ﷺ and what he brought, the Qur'an and the resurrection.1,2,3,13,14 One report traces the occasion to four men of Banu ʿAmr ibn ʿUmayr, two of whom later accepted Islam, though another view takes the verse as addressing disbelievers generally.3

This denial is treated as settled character, not a passing lapse: rejection, stubbornness, and standing against the truth.4,5,6,10 Al-Saʿdī (d. 1957 CE) puts it plainly: someone who denies the truth out of pure obstinacy, after it has already become clear, cannot be reasoned with.5 Isrār Aḥmad (d. 2010 CE) draws a distinction between kufr and takdhīb. Kufr, he says, means concealing the inner testimony Allah placed within every person's nature. Takdhīb means denying the revealed signs sent to awaken that same testimony. On his reading takdhīb is the graver offence, since it comes after clear proof has arrived, leaving no excuse. He points to the charter given to Adam (عليه السلام), where the two wrongs, kafaru and kadhdhabu, are named separately.8

The next line turns to what is hidden inside them. 'Yūʿūna' is glossed by Mujahid as 'they conceal'.1,2,4,11,12 Qatada locates the concealment in their breasts, what they hide of denial despite knowing the truth, a sense echoed from Ibn ʿAbbās.1,3 Ibn Zayd reads the word through its root: as a person stores goods in a container, hearts are a vessel holding all deeds, good and bad, all known to Allah.1 Al-Qurṭubī (d. 1273 CE) traces the same root, al-wiʿāʾ, quoting a line of poetry that good endures while evil is 'the worst thing you can store as provision', and notes the word can also mean to memorise or retain.3 Al-Saʿdī reads it as their secret deeds and intentions, all known to Allah alongside what is open, with recompense to follow.5,12 Ṭanṭāwī (d. 2010 CE) calls the clause a parenthetical insertion, meant as threat and warning.9 Isrār Aḥmad adds that the common reading, that this is about hoarding wealth, misses the point. He takes it as the impurity filling their hearts, disbelief, enmity, envy, arrogance, which explains their denial even after recognising the truth.8

Then comes the instruction to 'give them tidings'. Al-Qurṭubī and Ṭanṭāwī both read this as bitter irony: the word normally announces good news, here it announces painful torment.3,9 Al-Saʿdī notes that bishāra is named for its effect on the bashara, the skin, whether that effect is joy or grief, so the word properly fits pain as well as pleasure. He adds that this describes the state of most people: denying the Qur'an and lacking faith in it.5 Sayyid Quṭb (d. 1966 CE) calls it the worst kind of good news, one with no joy in it, that nobody wants and nobody waits for, set against the reward prepared for those who believe and are exempted through righteous deeds.6 The command falls to the Prophet ﷺ himself: he is told to inform the deniers of the painful punishment Allah has prepared for them.1,4,13,14

Their denial is not a lack of evidence but a chosen posture, and Allah, who knows what their hearts store away, meets that posture with a warning dressed, ironically, as good news.3,5,6,9

84:25.title: The Never-Ending Reward
84:25.in_short: After describing the fate awaiting the disbelievers, the surah's last verse turns to those who believed and did good, promising them a reward that will never be cut off.

claims.text: This verse excludes believers who did righteous deeds from the painful punishment just described for those who deny the truth; the sentence marks a clear turn from warning to promise.

sources.original_excerpt: إلا الذين تابوا منهم وصدّقوا
This is a clear exception meaning, `but those who believe.'

claims.text: Grammatically the exception is a 'discontinuous exception' (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ): believers were never really part of the group being threatened, so the sense is 'but' rather than a literal carving-out from the same set.

sources.original_excerpt: استثناء منقطع
استثناء منقطع
عربی زبان میں اسے استثنائے منقطع کیا جاتا ہے

original_terms.gloss: an exception that breaks from, rather than truly subtracts from, the preceding group

claims.text: Some scholars, as reported by al-Qurṭubī, held that the word 'illā' here does not function as an exception at all, but simply carries the meaning of 'and' — as if the verse said 'and those who believed and did good deeds...'

sources.original_excerpt: وإنما هو بمعنى الواو

claims.text: Ibn Kathīr draws a distinction: 'those who believe' refers to belief held in the heart, while 'and do righteous deeds' refers to the corresponding actions carried out with the limbs.

sources.original_excerpt: This refers to those who believe in their hearts... referring to that which they do with their limbs.

claims.text: The word 'mamnūn' comes from the root m-n-n, which means to cut — as in 'I cut the rope' (mananta al-ḥabl) — so 'ghayr mamnūn' means a reward that will never be cut off or come to an end.

sources.original_excerpt: يقال : مننت الحبل : إذا قطعته
مِنْ مَنَّ : إذا قطع
مَنَّ یَمُنُّ مَنًّا کے لغوی معنی کسی چیز کو کاٹ دینے کے ہیں

claims.text: Ibn ʿAbbās رضي الله عنه is reported as glossing 'ghayr mamnūn' as 'not decreased' (ghayr manqūṣ), a reading also carried by al-Baghawī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, and al-Muyassar.

sources.original_excerpt: يقول: غير منقوص
غير مقطوع ولا منقوص
غير منقوص ولا مقطوع
Without being decreased.
غير مقطوع ولا منقوص

report.graded_by: al-Ṭabarī (chain relayed without formal grading)

claims.text: Mujāhid, and also al-Ḍaḥḥāk in Ibn Kathīr's report, glossed 'ghayr mamnūn' as 'without measure' or 'not counted' (ghayr maḥsūb), meaning the reward is beyond calculation.

sources.original_excerpt: يعني: غير محسوب
Mujahid and Ad-Dahhak both said, "Without measure."

report.graded_by: al-Ṭabarī / Ibn Kathīr (chains relayed without formal grading)

claims.text: Ibn Kathīr reports that al-Suddī combined both readings, saying the phrase means the reward is 'without end and without decrease' at once, and notes the sense parallels Qurʾān 11:108, 'a gift without end.'

sources.original_excerpt: without end and without decrease

report.graded_by: Ibn Kathīr (relaying al-Suddī without formal grading)

claims.text: Al-Qurṭubī reports that when Nāfiʿ ibn al-Azraq asked Ibn ʿAbbās whether the Arabs knew this sense of 'mamnūn' as 'cut off', Ibn ʿAbbās cited a verse of poetry by a man of the Yashkur tribe, who used 'manīn' for the dust that trails and is cut off behind galloping animals; al-Mubarrad explained that any weak or thin thing is described this way because it is easily severed.

sources.original_excerpt: فترى خلفهن من سرعة الرجع منينا كأنه أهباء

original_terms.gloss: trailing dust, so called because it is cut off behind

report.graded_by: al-Qurṭubī (linguistic athar, not formally graded)

claims.text: A second gloss for 'ghayr mamnūn' is that the reward is free of any sense of a favour held over the recipient's head, unlike a human gift that is given and then boasted about.

sources.original_excerpt: لا يمن عليهم به
خالص من شوائب الامتنان

claims.text: Al-Saʿdī describes the reward of those who believed and did what the messengers brought as a lasting reward, unlike anything an eye has seen, an ear has heard, or a human heart has imagined.

sources.original_excerpt: مما لا عين رأت، ولا أذن سمعت، ولا خطر على قلب بشر

claims.text: Sayyid Quṭb notes the exception marks out those who were excluded from the grim tidings as extremely fortunate, and observes that the surah reaches its decisive close on this note of an unending reward.

sources.original_excerpt: جن لوگوں کو مستثنیٰ کیا گیا وہ بہت ہی خوش قسمت ہیں

claims.text: Wahiduddin Khan reads the verse as the surah's conclusion: those who respond positively to the call of truth, despite facing hardship and opposition, receive the greatest possible reward from the Merciful God.

84:25.essay_html:
The surah closes by turning from warning to promise. Everything said before this verse concerned those who deny the truth and refuse to bow before the Qurʾān; now the text sets apart those who believed and did righteous deeds.1,2,3,4,9,13,14,11,12

Grammarians look closely at the word 'except' (illā) here. Several commentators call it a discontinuous exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ): believers were never truly part of the group under threat, so the sense runs closer to 'but' than to a literal carving-out.3,9,6 Al-Qurṭubī also records that some scholars read illā here as simply meaning 'and', so the sentence would run as 'and those who believed and did righteous deeds...'3 Ibn Kathīr adds a further distinction inside the verse itself: belief belongs to the heart, while righteous deeds are what the limbs carry out.4

The heart of the verse is the phrase 'ghayr mamnūn' — a reward that is never cut off. The word mamnūn comes from a root meaning 'to cut', as in cutting a rope, so the phrase promises a reward that will never be severed or brought to an end.3,9,8 Early exegetes glossed the phrase in two directions. Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said it means 'not decreased', a reading also carried by al-Baghawī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, and al-Muyassar.1,2,3,4,13 Mujāhid, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk according to Ibn Kathīr, glossed it as 'without measure' or 'uncounted', meaning the reward is beyond reckoning.1,4 Ibn Kathīr further reports that al-Suddī combined both senses, saying the reward is without end and without decrease at once, and compares the phrase to the promise elsewhere in the Qurʾān of 'a gift without end'.4

Al-Qurṭubī preserves a linguistic exchange: Nāfiʿ ibn al-Azraq asked Ibn ʿAbbās whether the Arabs actually used mamnūn to mean 'cut off'. Ibn ʿAbbās answered by quoting a line of poetry from a man of Yashkur, who described trailing dust as 'manīn' because it is cut off behind galloping animals; al-Mubarrad explained that anything thin or weak is called by this word because it is easily severed.3 A second gloss offered for the phrase is that this reward carries no trace of the kind of favour a person holds over someone after giving a gift and then boasting of it.3,9

Al-Saʿdī describes the promised reward in the largest terms available to him: a lasting reward, unlike anything an eye has seen, an ear has heard, or a human heart has ever imagined.5 Sayyid Quṭb reads the exception itself as a mark of extraordinary good fortune, set against the dark tidings just given to the deniers, and notes that the surah reaches its decisive close on this very note.6 Wahiduddin Khan reads the verse as the surah's final word: whoever answers the call of truth, despite hardship and opposition, receives the greatest reward from the Merciful God.10

The surah that opened with the sky splitting apart ends on a single promise: for those who believed and acted rightly, the reward will never be cut off.

84:16.title: Oaths of Twilight, Night and Moon
84:16.in_short: God swears by the evening's afterglow, by the night that gathers everything into its fold, and by the moon growing full, that every person will pass through stage after stage of change. The passage then asks why, given all this, the deniers still will not believe or bow when the Qur'an is read to them.

claims.text: Most commentators define al-shafaq as the red glow that lingers in the western sky after sunset, lasting until the time of the night (ʿIshāʾ) prayer.

sources.original_excerpt: هو الحمرة في الأفق من ناحية المغرب
الحمرة التي في المغرب
Ash-Shafaq is the redness

original_terms.gloss: the glow of dusk, the reddish light after sunset

claims.text: A minority, tracing to Mujāhid, held that al-shafaq means the daylight itself, not the after-sunset glow.

sources.original_excerpt: لا تقل الشفق، إن الشفق من الشمس، ولكن قل: حمرة الأفق ... النهار كله
هو النهار كله

claims.text: Others held al-shafaq is the whiteness that follows the red glow, rather than the redness itself.

sources.original_excerpt: Ash-Shafaq is the whiteness

claims.text: Because the redness (al-shafaq) marks the boundary of the sunset prayer's time, jurists tied the end of the Maghrib prayer window to its disappearance; this is reported as Mālik's position, among others.

sources.original_excerpt: فإذا ذهبت الحمرة فقد خرجت من وقت المغرب ووجبت صلاة العشاء
وَقْتُ الْمَغْرِبِ مَا لَمْ يَغِبِ الشَّفَق

report.graded_by: Muslim, as cited by Ibn Kathīr

claims.text: Al-Qurṭubī notes a linguistic kinship between shafaq (twilight glow) and shafaqah (tenderness, compassion of heart), since both describe something delicate and thin.

sources.original_excerpt: أصل الكلمة من رقة الشيء ... وأشفق عليه أي رق قلبه عليه

claims.text: Most commentators read 'the night and what it wasaqa' as: the night gathers up and folds in everything that was scattered by day, as every creature returns to its resting place.

sources.original_excerpt: وما جمع مما سكن وهدأ فيه من ذي روح
What it gathers

claims.text: ʿIkrimah and others read the same phrase differently: the night 'drives' everything into shelter with its darkness, so the sense is propulsion rather than mere gathering.

sources.original_excerpt: ما ساق من ظلمة، فإذَا كان الليل، ذهب كلّ شيء إلى مأواه
وما ساق من شيء إلى حيث يأوي
What it drives into due to its darkness

claims.text: The root of wasaqa is grounded in the image of a camel's load (wasq, a measure of about sixty ṣāʿ) - things bundled and carried together, which colours the reading of the night as gathering things into itself.

sources.original_excerpt: طعام موسُوق، وهو المجموع في غرائر أو وعاء، ومنه الوَسْق
إبل مستوسقة أي مجتمعة

claims.text: Sayyid Quṭb reads the scene of twilight sliding into night as an atmosphere of awe and hush: the human self feels a quiet dread as light withdraws and the darkness folds every living and hidden thing into itself.

sources.original_excerpt: غروب کے بعد نفس انسانی پر بھی ایک گہری خاموشی اور خوف کے سائے پڑجاتے ہیں

claims.text: The majority read 'the moon when it becomes complete (ittasaqa)' as the full moon of the fourteenth night, when its light is fully gathered.

sources.original_excerpt: إذا تمّ واستوى
أي تم واجتمع واستوى

original_terms.gloss: to become complete, gathered into fullness

claims.text: Qatādah read ittasaqa specifically as 'became round' (istadāra), completing its circuit.

sources.original_excerpt: إذا استدار
When it completes its cycle

claims.text: Isrār Aḥmad offers a distinctive symbolic reading of the sequence: he takes the fading of the shafaq, the darkening night, and the moon's gradual completion as an allegory for Islam's decline and its later gradual, generation-by-generation restoration, unlike its first swift rise under the Prophet ﷺ.

sources.original_excerpt: پہلی قسم ... میں اسلام کے رفتہ رفتہ زوال پذیر ہونے کی صورت حال کا نقشہ دکھایا گیا ہے

claims.text: There is a well-known difference in recitation of 'la-tarkabunna': one vowelling (fatḥah on the bāʾ) addresses the Prophet ﷺ alone; the other (ḍammah) addresses all mankind.

original_terms.gloss: 'you will surely ride/pass through' - fatḥah = Prophet addressed; ḍammah = mankind addressed

claims.text: On the reading addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, Ibn ʿAbbās (as related by Mujāhid, recorded by al-Bukhārī) explained ṭabaqan ʿan ṭabaq as 'state after state', meaning the Prophet ﷺ himself would pass through one condition after another.

sources.original_excerpt: لَتَرْكَبَنَّ طَبَقًا عَنْ طَبَقٍ يعني نبيكم صلى الله عليه وسلم حالا بعد حال
Stage after stage. Your Prophet has said this.
حَالًا بَعْدَ حَالٍ

report.graded_by: al-Bukhārī, as noted by Ibn Kathīr

claims.text: Al-Shaʿbī and Mujāhid, on the same fatḥah reading, took it to mean 'heaven after heaven' - the Prophet ﷺ ascending through the skies.

sources.original_excerpt: سماء بعد سماء

claims.text: Ibn Masʿūd, on the fatḥah reading, took it to refer instead to the sky itself changing state at the Hour - splitting apart, turning red, becoming like molten matter or oil.

sources.original_excerpt: السماء مرّة كالدِّهان، ومرّة تَشَقَّق

claims.text: On the ḍammah reading, addressed to mankind generally, the meaning is that people will pass through state after state of hardship, since the surrounding verses speak of people broadly; al-Ṭabarī states this is the reading he judges correct, though understood as covering the whole of humanity's trials at the Resurrection.

sources.original_excerpt: والصواب من التأويل قول من قال لَتَرْكَبَنَّ أنت يا محمد حالا بعد حال ... والمراد بذلك ... جميع الناس

claims.text: Several commentators unpack the 'stages' concretely as the stages of a human life: nursing infant, then weaned child, then youth, then old age (ʿIkrimah); or as ease alternating with hardship, wealth with poverty, health with sickness (al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī).

sources.original_excerpt: حالا بعد حال، فطيما بعد رضيع، وشيخا بعد شباب
Ease after difficulty, difficulty after ease

claims.text: Ibn ʿAbbās is also reported (in another transmission) to have taken the stages as the terrors of death, then resurrection, then the standing before God (al-ʿarḍ); Ibn Zayd took them as passing from this world's stage to the stage of the next world.

sources.original_excerpt: الشدائد والأهوال: الموت، ثم البعث، ثم العرض
الآخرة بعد الأولى

claims.text: Later commentators (al-Saʿdī, Muftī Shafīʿ, Abū Bakr Zakariyyā) read the 'stages' as the embryological and life journey: sperm-drop, clinging clot, lump of flesh, ensoulment, then infancy, moral responsibility, death, and finally resurrection and reckoning - a chain of change showing man's dependence on God who alone governs him with wisdom and mercy.

sources.original_excerpt: من النطفة إلى العلقة، إلى المضغة، إلى نفخ الروح

claims.text: A hadith is cited (via Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, recorded by al-Bukhārī) in which the Prophet ﷺ said the community would follow the ways of those before them 'span by span, cubit by cubit', to the point that companions asked whether this meant the Jews and Christians, and he said 'who else?' - cited as an illustration of passing through successive stages/conditions.

sources.original_excerpt: لتتبعن سنن من كان قبلكم شبرا شبرا وذراعا ذراعا

report.graded_by: al-Bukhārī, as cited by al-Qurṭubī

claims.text: A report attributed to the Prophet ﷺ, transmitted through Jābir b. ʿAbdullāh via Abū Nuʿaym, describes the successive stages of a person's life-writing by the angels - destiny recorded, then guarded, then deeds recorded, then death, then the two angels of the grave, then resurrection - with the Prophet ﷺ then reciting this verse and adding 'ahead of you is a great matter, so seek help from God the Great'.

sources.original_excerpt: إن ابن آدم لفي غفلة عما خلقه الله

report.graded_by: al-Qurṭubī, who cites it via Abū Nuʿaym without further grading

claims.text: Al-Qurṭubī treats this constant change of human states as itself proof of a Creator, citing a saying (attributed to Abū Bakr al-Warrāq) that the very fact of a person being in one condition today and another tomorrow shows that his affairs are directed by another.

sources.original_excerpt: تحويل الحالات، وعجز القوة، وضعف الأركان، وقهر النية، ونسخ العزيمة

claims.text: Linguistically, ṭabaq is also the Arabic idiom for falling into a severe, dire matter (as in the expression 'banāt ṭabaq' for calamity), which colours the sense of hardship in the phrase.

sources.original_excerpt: وقع فلان في بنات طبق: إذا وقع في أمر شديد
وقع في أمر شديد ... أم طبق

claims.text: Isrār Aḥmad extends his symbolic reading here: just as the moon fills stage by stage, the community will rise to the dominance of religion through gradual, generational effort rather than in one sudden burst as happened in the Prophet's ﷺ own lifetime.

sources.original_excerpt: اسلام کے دوسرے غلبہ کی روشنی چاند کی چاندنی کی طرح مرحلہ وار اور تدریجاً پھیلے گی

claims.text: 'So why do they not believe?' is read as a rhetorical question of reproach: nothing genuinely prevents belief once the proofs have been made plain, so the question exposes the unreasonableness of their denial.

sources.original_excerpt: استفهام إنكار
استفهام إنكار ... تعجب

claims.text: Ibn Zayd specifies that the disbelief in question is disbelief in 'this discourse and this matter', that is, in the Qur'an and in what it tells of resurrection.

sources.original_excerpt: بهذا الحديث، وبهذا الأمر

claims.text: Their refusal to believe and to bow before the Qur'an is treated as deserving of the punishment already described earlier in the surah.

'They do not prostrate' is understood by commentators as meaning they do not submit, do not humble themselves, and do not obey what the Qur'an commands and forbids - not merely a failure of ritual bowing.

sources.original_excerpt: لا يخضعون ولا يستكينون
لا يصلون
لا يصلون
لا يخضعون للقرآن، ولا ينقادون لأوامره ونواهيه

claims.text: This verse is counted among the places where prostration upon recitation (sujūd al-tilāwah) is practised, supported by the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, who prostrated on reciting it and said he had seen the Prophet ﷺ do the same, adding he would keep prostrating at it until he met him.

sources.original_excerpt: سجدنا مع رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - في اقرأ باسم ربك وإذا السماء انشقت

report.graded_by: Muslim and al-Bukhārī, as cited by the commentators

claims.text: Jurists differ on the ruling of this prostration: Abū Ḥanīfah held it obligatory; al-Shāfiʿī held it a recommended sunnah; Mālik's considered position, as reported, is that this verse is not among the specific verses of prostration, since here the sense is submission and obedience rather than the technical bodily prostration.

sources.original_excerpt: إنها ليست من عزائم السجود ... والصحيح أنها منه
وهى سنة عند الشافعى، وواجبة عند أبى حنيفة

claims.text: Ibn al-ʿArabī reportedly avoided reciting this surah when leading prayer, since he held prostration obligatory here but feared that whichever way he acted, the congregation - who followed a different view - would take offence.

sources.original_excerpt: إني إن سجدت أنكروه، وإن تركتها كان تقصيرا مني

claims.text: Some Ḥanafī jurists argued the definite article in 'the Qur'an' (al-Qurʾān) here refers back to this specific verse rather than the whole Qur'an, which would localise the obligation of prostration to this passage; Muftī Shafīʿ regards this reading as possible but far-fetched given the context.

84:16.essay_html:
The passage opens with three oaths drawn from the turn of day into night: the glow of dusk (al-shafaq), the night that gathers all things into itself, and the moon growing full. Most commentators take al-shafaq as the red light that lingers after sunset until nightfall proper, though Mujāhid took it instead as the daylight itself, and others as the whiteness that follows the redness.1,2,3,4,13 Because this glow marks the boundary of an evening prayer, jurists tied the end of the Maghrib prayer's time to its disappearance.3,4 Al-Qurṭubī notes that shafaq shares its root with shafaqah, tenderness of heart, both words carrying a sense of something delicate.3

'The night and what it wasaqa' is read by most as the night gathering and folding in everything that scattered by day, each creature returning to its resting place.1,2,3,4,5,7,9,13 ʿIkrimah read the same word as 'drives', so the night pushes things into shelter rather than merely gathering them.1,2,3,4 The root itself pictures a camel's load, things bundled together for carrying.1,3 Sayyid Quṭb (d. 1966) lingers on the mood of the scene: as light withdraws, a quiet dread and hush settles over the human self, echoing the stillness of the twilight before it.6

The moon 'when it is complete' (ittasaqa) is taken by the majority as the moon of the fourteenth night, its light fully gathered into fullness, while Qatādah reads it as the moon 'completing its circuit'.1,2,3,4,5,7,9,11,13 Isrār Aḥmad (d. 2010) reads the whole sequence - fading twilight, deepening night, growing moon - as an allegory: Islam's decline, and then its restoration by slow degrees rather than the sudden dawn of its first rise.8

The oath's answer is that mankind 'will surely pass, stage after stage' (ṭabaqan ʿan ṭabaq). The reciters differ on a single vowel: one reading addresses the Prophet ﷺ alone, the other addresses all people.1,2,3,9 On the first reading, Ibn ʿAbbās (as related by Mujāhid and recorded by al-Bukhārī) explained it as the Prophet ﷺ passing through 'state after state'; al-Shaʿbī and Mujāhid took it as heaven after heaven, referring to his ascension; Ibn Masʿūd took it instead as the sky itself changing state at the Hour, splitting, reddening, turning molten.1,2,3,4,9,14 On the second reading, favoured by al-Ṭabarī (d. 923) himself though he keeps the fatḥah wording, the meaning covers the whole of mankind's passage through hardship, since the surrounding verses speak of people generally.1,2,3,9

Commentators fill in what these 'stages' concretely mean in several different ways: infancy through weaning to youth and old age (ʿIkrimah); ease alternating with hardship, wealth with poverty, health with sickness (al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī); the terrors of death followed by resurrection and the standing before God (one report from Ibn ʿAbbās); or passing from the stage of this world to the stage of the next (Ibn Zayd).1,2,3,4 Later commentators such as al-Saʿdī (d. 1957), Muftī Shafīʿ (d. 1976) and Abū Bakr Zakariyyā trace the same word through the embryonic journey - a drop, a clinging clot, a lump of flesh, then the breathing-in of the soul, then infancy, responsibility, death, and finally resurrection - reading the whole chain as proof that man is dependent and God alone governs him with wisdom and mercy.5,7,11,13 Al-Qurṭubī (d. 1273) goes further, treating this constant alternation of states as itself an argument for a Creator, citing the saying that a person's condition changing from day to day shows his affairs are directed by Another.3 A hadith recorded by al-Bukhārī is cited alongside this verse, in which the Prophet ﷺ warned that the community would follow the ways of those before them 'span by span, cubit by cubit'.2,3,11 A further report, transmitted through Jābir b. ʿAbdullāh via Abū Nuʿaym and left ungraded by al-Qurṭubī, describes the angels recording a person's fate, then his deeds, then his death, resurrection following, with the Prophet ﷺ reciting this verse and adding: 'ahead of you is a great matter, so seek help from God the Great.'3,7 Isrār Aḥmad extends his earlier reading here too: as the moon fills stage by stage, so too will the community rise to the dominance of religion gradually, generation after generation.8

Against this backdrop the question follows: 'so why do they not believe?' Commentators read it as a rhetorical reproach, exposing that nothing genuinely stands between the deniers and belief once the proofs have been set out so plainly.1,2,3,4,9,13 Ibn Zayd specifies the disbelief in view as disbelief in 'this discourse', the Qur'an and its report of resurrection.1 Their stance is treated as deserving of the punishment already described earlier in the surah.10

The closing charge, that they 'do not prostrate' when the Qur'an is read to them, is read by the commentators as meaning something wider than physical bowing: they do not submit, do not humble themselves, do not obey what it commands and forbids.1,2,3,5,9,13 This verse is nonetheless counted among the places of prostration upon recitation, on the strength of Abū Hurayrah's report that he prostrated at it because he had seen the Prophet ﷺ do so, and that he would keep doing it until he met him.2,3,4,9,7,11,12,14 Jurists differ on whether this prostration is obligatory: Abū Ḥanīfah held that it is, al-Shāfiʿī treated it as a recommended sunnah, and Mālik's reported view held that this particular verse is not among the specific verses of prostration at all, since its sense is obedience rather than the ritual act.3,7,9 Ibn al-ʿArabī is said to have avoided reciting this surah in congregational prayer altogether, caught between his own view that the prostration was obligatory and his fear of the congregation's objection whichever way he acted.3 Some Ḥanafī jurists went further still, arguing that 'the Qur'an' in this verse points back grammatically to this very passage rather than the whole Book, though Muftī Shafīʿ (d. 1976) judges this reading far-fetched.7

The commentators read these oaths of dusk, night and moon as a mirror of man's own passage, one state always giving way to the next, and they take the closing question as laying bare that it is not evidence that is lacking, but the will to bow.1,3,5,9

84:6.title: Toiling to Meet Your Lord
84:6.in_short: Every human being is toiling on a journey that ends before God; two very different endings are then described, one for the person who receives good news in the right hand, one for the person who receives it from behind his back, and the passage closes by exposing why the second one is where he is: a false certainty that he would never have to answer.

claims.text: Kadḥ (toil) means to spend full effort and strain in a task, whether the deed done is good or bad; the phrase pictures every human being as constantly striving toward an encounter with his Lord.

original_terms.gloss: hard exertion, effort spent to the point of strain

claims.text: "O man" is read by most as addressing the whole human race, believer and disbeliever alike; some named it as revealed about a particular disbeliever (al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd al-Asad, or Ubayy ibn Khalaf), or about disbelievers as a group, though the general reading is favoured.

The pronoun in "you will meet it/him" is read two ways: you will meet your Lord (who repays the effort), or you will meet the toil itself (its consequence, good or bad); commentators note the two readings amount to the same thing, since meeting the deed is meeting its reward from the Lord.

A hadith is cited in which Jibrīl عليه السلام told the Prophet ﷺ: "live as you wish, for you will die; love what you wish, for you will part from it; do as you wish, for you will meet it" — used to support the idea that a person meets the consequence of his own deeds.

report.graded_by: not graded in the cited sources

claims.text: Qatādah is reported as saying: your toil, son of Adam, is weak indeed, so whoever can make his toil toil spent in obedience to Allah should do so.

Sayyid Quṭb reads the address as recalling that man alone among creation was given a soul and a capacity that lets him reach toward his Lord and rise to spiritual heights beyond any other creature, so the toil described here is the toil of that unique, upward-facing nature.

Isrār Aḥmad contrasts man with a burden-bearing animal: an ox worked to death is freed from its toil by dying, but man's toil does not end with death, it continues into a full accounting before his Lord for every moment of his life.
Receiving one's record in the right hand marks the believer, the person of true faith.

ʿĀʾishah رضي الله عنها reported that the Prophet ﷺ said "whoever is scrutinised in the reckoning will be punished/destroyed"; when she asked about this verse's "easy reckoning," he explained that the easy reckoning is merely a presentation (al-ʿarḍ) before Allah, without cross-examination — whoever's account is picked apart in detail is ruined.

report.graded_by: Bukhārī and Muslim (noted by al-Qurṭubī, source 3); also recorded by Tirmidhī, who called it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ

claims.text: A separate report from ʿĀʾishah has the Prophet ﷺ praying in his prayer, "Allah, reckon with me an easy reckoning," and explaining afterward that this means his record will be looked at and then overlooked.

report.graded_by: not graded in the cited sources

claims.text: Ibn Zayd read the "easy reckoning" as meaning the person's sins are forgiven and his good deeds accepted, linking it to other verses about Allah overlooking the sins of the people of Paradise.

al-Saʿdī describes the easy reckoning as Allah confronting the servant with his sins privately until he thinks he is ruined, then telling him: I concealed this for you in the world, and I conceal it for you today.

report.graded_by: not graded by al-Saʿdī

claims.text: "Return to his people, well pleased" is read by most as returning, in Paradise, to a family prepared for him there (including the houris) — the primary reading, attributed among others to Qatādah.
An alternative reading takes "his people" as his worldly family, present at the gathering, to whom he returns to announce, in the manner of this life, the good news of his success.
It is said that this verse was revealed concerning Abū Salamah ibn ʿAbd al-Asad, the first Meccan to migrate to Madinah.

Receiving the record "from behind the back" is pictured physically: the right hand is bound or twisted up behind the neck, so the record can only be taken with the left hand from behind the back — some added that the forearm is forced through the chest and out the back.
Isrār Aḥmad reads the scene as the man himself hiding his left hand behind his back to avoid taking the record, and it is thrust into that hand anyway.
It is said this verse was revealed about al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd al-Asad, brother of Abū Salamah, on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās, and then applies generally to every believer and disbeliever.
"Calling for thubūr" means crying out for his own destruction and ruin, shouting "O my ruin, O my destruction" as if summoning his own annihilation.

original_terms.gloss: ruin, destruction; a cry of despair

claims.text: Sayyid Quṭb and al-Ṭanṭāwī both cite a line of poetry (attributed to al-Mutanabbī) that it is the extreme of misery when a man comes to see death itself as a cure, and destruction as a wish rather than a fear.

The verb describing entry into the fire is read two or three ways among the Qurʾan-reciters: one reading (doubled, intensive) pictures repeated burning, being cast in again and again; the other (simple) pictures entering and being scorched by it; scholars judge both readings sound and each correctly conveyed.

original_terms.gloss: he is (repeatedly) burned / he burns, enters the fire

claims.text: "He was, among his people, well pleased" refers to worldly joy, heedless of the reckoning to come; he gave no thought to consequences and made no preparation.

Ibn Zayd drew a contrast: Allah described the people of Paradise as having lived in fear, sorrow and weeping in this world, rewarded afterward with bliss; and described the people of the Fire as having lived in joy and laughter in this world, met afterward with punishment.
"He thought he would never return" means he was convinced he would not be resurrected or brought back to his Lord, so he felt no need to fear punishment or hope for reward.

Lexically, the root of yaḥūr means "to return"; al-Qurṭubī cites Labīd's line about a meteor's light returning to ash, and an anecdote where Ibn ʿAbbās رضي الله عنه says he only learned the word's sense on hearing a Bedouin woman call her daughter back with "ḥawrī" (come back to me). Some also said it was an Abyssinian word meaning "return."

original_terms.gloss: to return / a returning, a reverting

claims.text: The Prophet's ﷺ supplication, "Allah, I seek refuge in You from al-ḥawr after al-kawr" (reverting to loss after gain, i.e. to disbelief after faith), is cited as linguistic and theological confirmation that ḥawr means a reverting or turning back.

report.graded_by: cited as in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim by source 12 (Ahsanul Bayaan)

claims.text: "Yes indeed!" directly refutes the man's assumption: he will in fact return and be resurrected, contrary to what he believed.

"His Lord was ever watching him" is read as Allah's complete knowledge of him from the day of his creation to his resurrection; al-Saʿdī adds the reasoning that it would not befit Allah to leave a person without command or prohibition, without reward or punishment.

84:6.essay_html:
Every human life, the commentators say, is a long exertion (kadḥ) toward an appointment, believer and disbeliever alike toil, and the toil ends before the Lord.1,2,3,4,5,9,11,12,13,14 Some read "O man" as addressed to a particular disbeliever at the time of revelation, but most take it as addressed to the whole human race.3,12 Grammarians note the closing pronoun could mean "you will meet your Lord" or "you will meet the toil itself", and observe the two readings come to the same thing, since meeting the deed is meeting its reward from Him.1,4,7,9 A hadith about Jibrīl عليه السلام telling the Prophet ﷺ to live, love, and act as he wishes, "for you will meet it", is brought to support this.4,9 Qatādah is remembered saying that since a man's toil is weak, let it at least be toil spent in obeying Allah.1,3 Sayyid Quṭb (d. 1966) reads the address as recalling man's unique standing among creation, a being given a soul capable of reaching upward toward his Lord.6 Isrār Aḥmad (d. 2010) contrasts man with a burden-animal: an ox's toil ends with its death, but man's toil continues into a full reckoning after death.8

Two records, two very different receptions. The record given in the right hand marks the believer.3,9,11,12,13 His reckoning is called "easy", and a well-known report from ʿĀʾishah رضي الله عنها explains what that means: the Prophet ﷺ said that whoever's account is picked apart in scrutiny is ruined, and that the "easy reckoning" of this verse is merely a presentation before Allah, without cross-examination.1,2,3,4,7,8,9,11,12 A related report has the Prophet ﷺ praying for an easy reckoning himself, explained the same way, as a record looked at and then passed over.1,2,9 Ibn Zayd took the ease to mean forgiveness of sin and acceptance of good deeds,1 and al-Saʿdī (d. 1957) pictures Allah reminding the servant privately of sins no one else knew of, then telling him, "I concealed it for you in the world, and I conceal it for you today."5 This believer then "returns to his people, well pleased", most read this as a family already prepared for him in Paradise, though some hold it means his worldly family, to whom he brings the good news, in the manner of this life.2,3,5,7,9,11,12,14 One report ties the verse to Abū Salamah, the first Meccan to migrate to Madinah.3

The other man receives his record from behind his back. Commentators picture his right hand bound or twisted up behind his neck, so the record can only reach him, from behind, in his left hand.1,2,3,9 Isrār Aḥmad reads it as the man himself hiding his hand to avoid taking it, in vain.8 One report names this verse for al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd al-Asad, before applying generally to every disbeliever.3 He then "calls for destruction" (thubūr), crying out his own ruin as if summoning it.1,2,3,9,11,12 Sayyid Quṭb and al-Ṭanṭāwī (d. 2010) both quote a line of poetry: it is the height of misery when a man comes to wish for death as a cure.6,9 The reciters differ, soundly, on how the verb for entering the fire is read, one picturing repeated burning, the other simply entering and being scorched.1,2,3

Why did he end here? "He was, among his people, well pleased" in this world, heedless of any reckoning to come.1,2,3,4,7,8,9,13,14 Ibn Zayd drew the contrast sharply: the people of Paradise lived this life in fear and weeping, rewarded afterward with bliss; the people of the Fire lived this life in laughter and joy, met afterward with punishment.3 The root of it was a false certainty, "he thought he would never return", convinced he would not be raised or brought back to his Lord.1,2,3,4,9,11,12,13,14 Al-Qurṭubī traces the word for "return" (yaḥūr) through the poet Labīd's image of a meteor's light returning to ash, and an anecdote where Ibn ʿAbbās رضي الله عنه says he only grasped the word on hearing a Bedouin woman call her daughter back to her.3 The Prophet's ﷺ own prayer for refuge from "reverting to loss after gain" is cited for the same sense of turning back.1,3,9,12 Against that false certainty comes the answer: "Yes indeed!" He will return, he will be resurrected.1,2,3,4,9,11,12,13 And the reason given is simple, his Lord was watching him the entire time, knowing him fully from the day of his creation onward, and, as al-Saʿdī puts it, it would not befit Allah to leave a person without command, without reward, without consequence.1,2,3,5,9

Two men toiled through the same world; one returns to his people rejoicing at an easy presentation of his record, the other calls out for his own ruin, and the difference the commentators trace back to a single false thought, that he would never have to return.

84:1.title: The Sky Splits, the Earth Obeys
84:1.in_short: This opening describes the Day of Resurrection breaking the sky apart and stretching the earth flat, both obeying their Lord's command as is rightly due from them, while the earth also throws out everything buried within it — the dead and its hidden treasures — until it stands completely empty.

claims.text: The splitting of the sky described here is a sign belonging to the Day of Judgement / the Resurrection, when the sky cracks apart and its order is disturbed.

Some reports describe the sky splitting open with clouds emerging from it (attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās), while ʿAlī رضي الله عنه is reported to have said it splits from the Milky Way, which he called the 'gate of heaven'.

report.graded_by: al-Qurṭubī relays without grading

claims.text: The surah is agreed to be Makkan.
It is reported that Abū Hurayrah رضي الله عنه, and before him the Prophet ﷺ, prostrated on reciting this verse, which is why this passage is treated as a place of prostration during recitation.

report.graded_by: Ibn Kathīr, citing Muslim, al-Nasā'ī and al-Bukhārī

claims.text: Linguistically, 'adhinat' comes from the root meaning 'to listen, give ear' (adhn), not from 'permission' (idhn), supported by the hadith that God 'listens' to no one's Qur'an recitation as He listens to a prophet chanting it, and by a line of Arabic poetry using the same sense.

report.graded_by: cited as a well-known hadith by al-Ṭabarī and others

claims.text: 'Adhinat li-rabbihā' means the sky heard and obeyed its Lord's command; the 'listening' spoken of here includes acting on what is heard, i.e. obedience.
'Wa ḥuqqat' means it was right and binding on the sky to obey, because it is entirely under the command of a Mighty Sovereign whose order cannot be refused or overcome.
Grammatically, 'wa ḥuqqat' is noted as a clause inserted between the conjoined verbs, rather than a plain continuation of the sentence.

Mufti Muhammad Shafi' distinguishes two kinds of divine command: legislated commands, which intelligent beings may freely obey or disobey, and cosmic/destined commands, which the whole universe follows by necessity. He suggests the sky and earth's 'listening' here may mean God grants them a special faculty of perception, like humans and jinn, so they freely submit — or it may simply describe the unbreakable cosmic decree, read figuratively as 'obedience'. He notes the wording leans toward the first sense.

Sayyid Qutb reads the passage rhetorically: the sky and earth are pictured as living, willing beings that hear Allah's command and submit at once, acknowledging His right over them without argument or hesitation. He notes the scene, despite depicting a vast cosmic upheaval, is drawn with calm and dignity, carrying a deep tone of balance and humility.
'Al-arḍu muddat' means the earth is stretched, spread out, and expanded in area.
A hadith image is used: the earth will be stretched out like tanned leather (al-adīm) until every fold and unevenness in it disappears.

report.graded_by: relayed by al-Baghawī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Saʿdī without a formal grading

claims.text: Mufti Muhammad Shafi' cites the same image via a hadith on the authority of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah رضي الله عنه, describing the earth stretched like leather with room only for each person's feet, which he notes was transmitted by al-Hakim with a good chain according to al-Mazharī.

report.graded_by: al-Mazharī, as cited by Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ

claims.text: The reason given for the earth being stretched is to make room for everyone from the first human to the last, all gathered at once for the reckoning, so that each person will have only enough space to place his feet.

As a result, the earth becomes a completely flat and level plain, with no crookedness or unevenness left, its mountains and buildings gone, comparable to the description elsewhere in the Qur'an of a smooth plain with no bends.
Mujahid is reported as specifying that this stretching of the earth takes place on the Day of Resurrection.

Sayyid Qutb observes that the verb 'muddat' is passive ('it is stretched'), suggesting the earth's change of shape comes from an outside cause suspending the laws that normally hold its current round or oval form.
'What is in it' cast out by the earth refers, in the primary reading, to the dead buried within it, brought up to its surface. This is attributed to Mujahid, Saʿīd, and Qatādah.
Other commentators add that 'what is in it' also includes treasures and minerals hidden within the earth, cast out alongside the dead.

Ibn Jubayr is reported to give a distinct division: 'cast out what is in it' refers to the dead from its belly, while 'became empty' refers to the earth being emptied of the living who were on its surface.

Further readings recorded by al-Qurṭubī: 'takhallat' (became empty) is also said to mean the earth is emptied of its mountains and seas, or that it gives up what it was entrusted with — the living and dead it held — and what it was charged to guard, its lands as a source of livelihood.
A simile is offered: the earth casting out what is within it resembles a pregnant woman expelling what is in her womb at a moment of severe distress.

Sayyid Qutb reads the earth here as pictured like a living being with a will of its own, vomiting out everything it has carried for ages: the uncountable dead buried across centuries, and the minerals, water, and secrets hidden in its depths known only to Allah, all disgorged at once when the Hour arrives.

The refrain is repeated for the earth: just as the sky obeyed, the earth too listens to and obeys its Lord's command to cast out what is within it, and this obedience is likewise its due, since it too is entirely under Allah's power.

Grammarians differ over the missing 'answer' clause to the two conditional 'when' statements ('when the sky is ripped apart... when the earth is levelled'). Views recorded include: the answer is simply omitted, understood from context (al-Ṭabarī's preferred reading, also noted by al-Baghawī and al-Qurṭubī); the answer is 'wa adhinat' itself, treating the 'and' as inserted (attributed to some grammarians, but al-Ṭabarī judges this merely an exegete's opinion not supported by Arabic usage, and al-Qurṭubī calls it a plain mistake); the answer is 'O man...' later in the surah, with an implied 'so' (noted by al-Baghawī and al-Qurṭubī); the answer is the later verse about the one given his record in his right hand, a view of al-Kisāʾī which al-Naḥḥās called the soundest opinion (per al-Qurṭubī); or the sentence order is rearranged, an approach attributed to al-Mubarrad.
Al-Ḥasan is reported to have held that 'when the sky is ripped apart' functions as an oath rather than a conditional; the majority disagree, holding it to be a statement, not an oath.

Wahiduddin Khan notes that what is described here about the Day of Judgement belongs to an unseen world, but its truth is supported by evidence such as the existence of the present world itself (which shows another world could likewise come to be) and by remarkable features of the Qur'an that testify it is the word of God.

84:1.essay_html:
This opening scene describes the sky splitting apart, a sign of the Day of Judgement1,2,3,4,9,11,12,13,14. Some report it splits open with clouds emerging, or, in a report from ʿAlī رضي الله عنه, from the Milky Way, which he called the gate of heaven3,13. The surah is agreed to be Makkan2,3,4,14, and it is reported that Abū Hurayrah رضي الله عنه and the Prophet ﷺ prostrated on reciting this verse, which is why it is treated as a place of prostration4,14.

The sky's response is described with two words. 'Adhinat' comes from the root for listening, not permission, a reading supported by a hadith about God 'listening' to a prophet's recitation and by a line of Arabic poetry1,3,9. So the sky heard its Lord's command and obeyed it, listening here meaning acting on what is heard1,2,4,5,7,8,11,12. 'Wa ḥuqqat' means this obedience was right and binding on it, because it stands entirely under a Mighty Sovereign whose order nothing can refuse or overcome1,3,4,5,9,11,12,14. Al-Ṭanṭāwī notes the phrase is grammatically inserted between the conjoined verbs9.

Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ (d. 1976) distinguishes two kinds of divine command: legislated commands, which intelligent beings may freely obey or defy, and cosmic commands, which the whole universe follows by necessity. He suggests the sky and earth's listening here might mean Allah grants them a faculty of perception like humans and jinn, so they submit willingly, though the cosmic reading remains possible figuratively7. Sayyid Quṭb (d. 1966) reads the whole scene rhetorically: sky and earth are pictured as living, willing beings acknowledging Allah's right over them and submitting without argument, and he notes the scene, for all its cosmic scale, is drawn with calm and dignity6.

The earth, too, is stretched and spread out1,2,3,5,7,9,11,12,14. A hadith image compares this to leather being stretched until every fold vanishes2,3,5,11; Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ cites a version on the authority of Jābir ibn ʿAbdullāh رضي الله عنه, graded good by al-Mazharī, in which there is only room for each person's feet7. The reason given is that everyone from the first human to the last will be gathered at once for the reckoning3,7,11. The result is a flat, level plain with no unevenness left, mountains and buildings gone2,5,7,11,12. Mujāhid is reported to specify this happens on the Day of Resurrection1. Sayyid Quṭb notes the verb is passive, 'it is stretched', hinting that some outside cause suspends the laws that normally hold the earth's shape6.

What the earth casts out is read, first, as the dead buried within it, attributed to Mujāhid, Saʿīd and Qatādah1,4. Others add treasures and minerals hidden inside it2,3,5,7,8,9,11,12,14. Ibn Jubayr is reported to divide the verse differently: the dead are cast out from its belly, while it is emptied of the living once on its surface3. Further readings recorded by al-Qurṭubī (d. 1273) take 'became empty' to mean stripped of its mountains and seas, or giving back what it was entrusted with and charged to guard3. A simile compares this to a pregnant woman expelling what is in her womb at a moment of distress3. Sayyid Quṭb pictures the earth as a living thing vomiting out everything it has carried for centuries, known in full only to Allah6.

The refrain returns for the earth: it too listens and obeys, and this obedience is equally its due1,4,8,12,13,14. Grammarians disputed where the 'answer' to these opening 'when' clauses actually falls, some leaving it understood from context, others locating it in 'wa adhinat', in the later address to man, or in the verse about the record given in the right hand, a view al-Naḥḥās is said to have judged soundest1,2,3. Al-Ḥasan is reported to have taken the opening clause as an oath, though the majority hold it to be simply a statement3.

Wahiduddin Khan (d. 2021) observes that what is described here belongs to an unseen world, yet its truth is supported by evidence available now, such as the very existence of this world, which shows another could likewise come to be10.

Sky and earth here are pictured, in the commentators' reading, less as inert matter than as creation itself giving Allah His due: hearing His command and submitting, because that submission was always rightly His.
